messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum is a 28-year-old man of European descent who works as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm. He lives with his long-term partner in a suburban apartment and, to outside observers, appears to be navigating a relatively ordinary civilian life. He was referred for psychological assessment after his partner encouraged him to seek help, having watched him become increasingly withdrawn over the past eighteen months.

Callum served two tours of duty before his honorable discharge at 25. The event that anchors his current presentation occurred during a vehicle patrol in his second tour, when the truck ahead of his was struck by an IED. He was among the first to reach the wreckage. What he found — the specific textures of torn flesh, the sound of a medevac helicopter arriving overhead, the helplessness of holding a wounded colleague while the rotors beat the air above — became encoded not as a coherent narrative but as a series of sensory shards. He describes his memories of that afternoon as arriving in disconnected pieces that refuse to assemble into a story he can hold: he might feel the full weight of that helplessness without any accompanying image, or a fragment of visual detail will surface without context. The event itself feels, to him, so extreme that he sometimes cannot fully accept it happened to him at all — which, paradoxically, makes it harder to process and easier for the fragments to ambush him.

In his current role, Callum manages content across several brand accounts and spends much of his working day scrolling through user-generated images. On more than one occasion he has encountered graphic photographs — accident footage, protest injuries, medical content — and the sight of visible wounds on others has plunged him immediately back into the sensory register of the patrol, triggering a surge of physical reactivity: racing heart, nausea, a cold sweat that he struggles to conceal in an open-plan office. Helicopter sounds — common in the city, whether from news crews or hospital flights — carry the same charge, cutting through whatever task he is engaged in and pulling him toward the wreckage. Driving with passengers has become its own ordeal; the particular vulnerability of sitting in a moving vehicle with others reactivates something he cannot fully name. Each of these triggers lands not merely as an unpleasant reminder but as evidence, to Callum, that he is permanently altered — that a person who had not been through what he endured would simply not react this way, and that someone stronger or more capable would not have found himself in that situation to begin with. This self-blame and the conviction that he is now fundamentally different from those around him feed back into his sensitivity: already primed by shame and the belief that he is an outsider, his nervous system meets the world at a lower threshold.

The hypervigilant state that now governs his body is most apparent at night, when the need to stay alert prevents him from falling asleep, and in public, where an unexpected touch — a colleague brushing his shoulder, his partner reaching for him in the dark — produces an alarm response that embarrasses and isolates him. This chronic physiological arousal has, over time, driven a set of strategies that Callum experiences as necessary management. He avoids any setting that might involve physical exertion or bodily stress, having learned that an elevated heart rate alone can be enough to trigger a cascade. He no longer attends the gym, has declined team-building activities, and has quietly stepped back from anything that might make his body feel like it is under demand. He will not walk past the police precinct near his office if he can help it, routing himself around it to avoid the sight of uniforms or holstered weapons. Before any social interaction — a meeting, a phone call, even a conversation with his partner about their weekend — he rehearses what he will say, constructing a careful script that keeps him in control and reduces the chance of being caught off guard. These strategies have kept him functional in a narrow sense, but they have also sealed the fragmented memories away from any processing, leaving them as raw and disorganised as they were in the weeks after his discharge. By avoiding the contexts in which memory might surface and integrate, Callum has inadvertently preserved their potency, so that when a trigger does break through, the physiological alarm is immediate and overwhelming. The avoidance itself has become a signal — to him and, increasingly, to those around him — that something is deeply wrong, reinforcing his belief that he is permanently damaged and cementing his sense of standing outside the life his partner and colleagues inhabit.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work when he encountered a graphic image he had not been able to flag in time, left his desk without explanation, and sat in a bathroom stall for forty minutes unable to return. His partner found him that evening still shaking. What Callum most fears is that this is simply who he is now. What he most hopes — tentatively, and with considerable doubt — is that he is wrong about that.
